name: Sparse Keyword Search (BM25)
question: Which documents contain these exact words?
summary: BM25 is the classic ranking function behind most keyword search engines. It scores a document by how often the query terms appear (with diminishing returns), how rare those terms are across the collection, and the document’s length. It needs no training, runs fast, and excels at exact matches.
useCases: Queries with error codes, SKUs, product names or people’s names
Technical jargon the embedding model has never seen
As the sparse half of a hybrid search

items.detail: rare terms count more than common ones
one dimension per vocabulary term, mostly zeros
SPLADE adds learned term expansion to the sparse idea

Index fields separately (title, body) and boost the important ones
Keep BM25 alongside vector search and fuse the results
Test on queries with codes, names and exact phrases
pitfalls: Keyword stuffing can game the ranking
remember: Exact words, rare terms, fast answers.

steps.title: Tokenize query and documents the same way
steps.text: Lowercase and split both with one analyzer. “E1045 login error” becomes three terms: e1045, login and error.

steps.title: Weigh each term by rarity (IDF)
steps.text: Across 1,000 documents, e1045 appears in 3, login in 120 and error in 300. Rare terms get the most weight: IDF 5.66 versus 1.20.

steps.title: Count term frequency, with saturation
steps.text: More occurrences help, but with diminishing returns. With k1 = 1.2 a term’s contribution can never exceed 2.2 times its IDF.

steps.title: Normalize for document length
steps.text: b = 0.75 scales the saturation point by document length, so a 420-word post doesn’t win just by containing more words.

steps.title: Rank the documents
steps.text: Sum the term scores per document. The short runbook with e1045 scores 14.5; the long blog post without it scores 5.8.

steps.title: Fuse with vector search
steps.text: Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1 ÷ (60 + rank) from each list. Exact matches from BM25 and paraphrase matches from vectors both surface.

pros: Exact matches on codes, IDs, names and rare jargon
No training or GPUs; fast on huge indexes
Explainable: you can see which terms matched and why
Built into Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Lucene and Postgres
cons: No understanding of synonyms or paraphrases
Sensitive to tokenization, stemming and language
Long, repetitive documents can still rank well
Keyword stuffing can game the ranking
avoidWhen: Users describe problems in their own words (add dense vectors)
Content is images or scans without text

practice.scenario: A support engineer searches “ERR_ORD_1045 order rejected”. Vector search returns general articles about order errors; BM25 returns the one runbook that contains that exact code.
practice.analogy: The index at the back of a textbook. Fast and exact for a word you know, no help if you don't know the word.

library.name: rank_bm25
library.what: Tiny pure-Python BM25 for learning and prototypes. In production the same scoring comes from Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Postgres.

samples.code:
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi

docs = ["Runbook ERR_ORD_1045 margin check failed at exchange gateway",
        "Common order errors and what they mean",
        "Login errors after a password reset"]
bm25 = BM25Okapi([d.lower().split() for d in docs])   # k1=1.5, b=0.75 by default

query = "err_ord_1045 margin rejected".split()
for score, doc in sorted(zip(bm25.get_scores(query), docs), reverse=True):
    print(f"{score:.2f}  {doc}")
# the runbook with the exact code ranks first

numericDrill.question: In 1,000 documents, “error” appears in 400 and “E1045” in 2. Using IDF ≈ ln(N ÷ df), how many times more does “E1045” weigh than “error”?
numericDrill.answer: ln(1000 ÷ 400) ≈ 0.92 and ln(1000 ÷ 2) ≈ 6.21, so “E1045” weighs about 6.8× more. (BM25's exact IDF formula differs slightly; the idea is the same.)

interview.question: Why keep BM25 when you have embeddings?
interview.answer: Embeddings blur exact tokens like error codes, SKUs, names and rare jargon, which BM25 matches precisely. Hybrid search combines both and usually beats either alone.

interview.question: What do k1 and b control in BM25?
interview.answer: k1 sets term-frequency saturation (how much repeats keep adding); b sets document-length normalization (0 none, 1 full). Typical values are k1 ≈ 1.2–2.0 and b ≈ 0.75.

mistakes.mistake: Different tokenization at index and query time
mistakes.fix: Use the same analyzer for both
Pair it with dense retrieval in a hybrid

quiz.question: Engineers search for “ERR_ORD_1045”, and vector search returns generic error articles. What is the fix?
options: Add BM25 and fuse it with vector search
quiz.explanation: Rare exact tokens are BM25’s strength. Hybrid search keeps both kinds of match.

quiz.question: A term appears in 10 of 10,000 case files. Using IDF = ln(N ÷ df), what is its IDF?
Why does the word “the” add almost nothing to a product’s BM25 score?
options: It is filtered by length normalization
Its IDF is tiny because it appears in almost every document
It is shorter than four characters
quiz.explanation: IDF rewards rare terms; a word in every document carries no signal.

quiz.question: Which setups can make BM25 miss documents that do contain the query terms? Select all that apply.
options: The index lowercases text but the query does not
Stemming is applied at index time but not at query time
The same analyzer is used for index and query
“UPI-ID” is split into different tokens at index and query time
quiz.explanation: Index and query must be tokenized identically. The same analyzer on both sides is the fix, not a cause.

quiz.question: What happens to BM25 scoring when k1 = 0?
options: Only whether a term appears matters, not how often
quiz.explanation: With k1 = 0 the term-frequency factor is 1 for any f > 0, so repeats add nothing.

quiz.question: A news archive sets b = 0. What changes?
options: Document length no longer affects scores, so long articles gain
quiz.explanation: b controls length normalization; b = 0 switches it off.

quiz.question: With k1 = 1.2 and a document of average length (b has no effect), what is the term-frequency factor f × (k1 + 1) ÷ (f + k1) for f = 3?
With k1 = 1.2, what is the most a single term’s frequency factor can ever reach, however often it repeats?
quiz.explanation: f × (k1 + 1) ÷ (f + k1 × (1 − b + b × len ÷ avgdl)) approaches k1 + 1 = 2.2 as f grows.

quiz.question: Which queries are better served by BM25 than by dense vectors? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Drug names, codes and record numbers are exact tokens. The symptom description is a meaning query.

quiz.question: A document is ranked 1st by BM25 and 3rd by vector search. With RRF and k = 60, what is its fused score?
Why fuse BM25 and vector results with reciprocal rank fusion instead of adding the raw scores?
options: RRF is more accurate by definition
The two scores are on very different, uncalibrated scales
Raw scores cannot be added in Python
quiz.explanation: BM25 scores are unbounded while cosine lies in [−1, 1]. RRF uses only ranks, so no calibration is needed.

quiz.question: A search for “car accident” misses judgments that only say “motor vehicle collision”. What addresses this?
options: Adding dense retrieval or learned sparse expansion alongside BM25
quiz.explanation: BM25 has no notion of synonyms. Dense vectors or a learned sparse model such as SPLADE add them.

quiz.question: Matches in shipment-manual titles matter more than matches in the body. What is the standard approach?
options: Index title and body as separate fields and boost the title
Repeat the title ten times in the body
Remove the body from the index
quiz.explanation: Per-field indexing with boosts expresses importance without distorting term frequencies.

quiz.question: Which statements describe SPLADE? Select all that apply.
options: It can add relevant terms the text does not contain
It can be served from an inverted index like BM25
quiz.explanation: SPLADE learns term weights and expansions but keeps the sparse, inverted-index form.

quiz.question: A payments team already runs Postgres and needs basic keyword search over dispute notes with no new infrastructure. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: Postgres full-text search runs next to the data. Note that its ts_rank ranking is not BM25.

quiz.question: A BM25 search for booking reference “X7K2PQ” misses a document that contains it. What is the most likely cause?
options: The IDF of the code is too high
Index and query analyzers tokenize the code differently
quiz.explanation: Codes are fragile under tokenization. Use the same analyzer, or a keyword field that keeps the code intact.

quiz.question: With b = 0.75, a 300-word document and an average length of 150 words, what is the length factor 1 − b + b × len ÷ avgdl?
A seller repeats “iphone” 50 times in a listing. Which part of BM25 limits the benefit?
quiz.explanation: Each extra occurrence adds less, so stuffing gains little beyond the first few repeats.

quiz.question: Which statements about IDF are true? Select all that apply.
options: Rare terms get a higher IDF
A term in every document gets an IDF close to 0 with Lucene’s formula
IDF depends on the length of the query
IDF is computed across the whole collection
quiz.explanation: IDF measures rarity across the collection; the query length does not affect it.

quiz.question: You are building a test set to compare BM25-only with hybrid search. What should it include? Select all that apply.
options: Queries containing error codes and ISINs
The known correct documents for every query
Only queries that already succeed today
quiz.explanation: Cover both failure types, with labelled answers. Only-successful queries hide the problems.
